intro: You notice a damp patch spreading across the wall in your hallway, or your water bill has crept up noticeably over the past couple of months — but there's no obvious dripping tap or burst pipe to explain it. For many homeowners in Temple, this is the first sign of a hidden leak. Whether it's a slow seep behind a stone wall or a pinhole in a pipe running under a concrete floor, leaks rarely fix themselves and almost always get worse. Getting a proper leak detection survey carried out sooner rather than later can save you a significant amount in repair bills, structural damage, and wasted water. Here's what the process involves and what you can expect to pay in Temple.
localContext: Temple is a small village in Midlothian with a mix of older stone-built properties, period cottages, and newer modern estates on the outskirts. Each property type comes with its own leak-related quirks. The thick stone walls of older Temple cottages are brilliant at hiding moisture — a pipe can weep for months before any visible sign appears on an interior surface, by which point the surrounding stonework may already be saturated. Older properties also tend to have pipework that hasn't been touched in decades, sometimes a mix of lead, copper, and plastic repairs carried out at different times, which creates more potential failure points. Modern estate homes in Temple are generally better protected but can still suffer from issues around buried supply pipes or faulty joints beneath floors. Temple sits in a moderately hard water area, which means limescale buildup is a genuine concern over time — scale deposits inside copper pipes can cause localised pressure stress and eventually contribute to pinhole leaks, particularly in hot water circuits.
serviceDetail: A professional leak detection visit in Temple typically begins with a conversation about what you've noticed — rising water usage, damp patches, sounds of running water when everything is turned off, or a drop in pressure. The plumber will start with a visual inspection of accessible pipework, checking joints, valves, and any previously repaired sections. If the leak isn't immediately obvious, they'll use specialist equipment to narrow it down. Acoustic listening devices can detect the sound of water escaping through a pipe even when it's buried in a wall or under a floor. Thermal imaging cameras are particularly useful in Temple's older stone properties, as they can pick up temperature changes caused by wet areas behind thick walls without needing to make any openings. Tracer gas testing — where a harmless gas is introduced into the pipe system and detected at the surface — is another method used for stubborn underground leaks. Once the leak is located, the plumber will talk you through the repair options before any work begins. Repair itself depends on what's found: it might be as straightforward as replacing a joint or section of pipe, or it may involve lifting a section of flooring or carefully opening a section of wall. In most cases the repair is completed in the same visit, and you'll be given clear advice on how to monitor the area afterwards.
pricing: In Temple, a leak detection survey typically costs in the region of £100 to £200, depending on how long the investigation takes and what equipment is needed. If the leak is found quickly and is in an accessible location, you're looking at the lower end of that range. Repairs on top of the detection work generally bring the total to somewhere between £150 and £500. Simple pipe joint repairs sit at the cheaper end, while work involving lifting floorboards, accessing buried pipework, or opening up sections of stonework in older Temple properties will naturally push costs higher. Most plumbers will give you a clear quote before any repair work begins, so you know exactly where you stand.
whyLocal: Choosing a tradesperson who knows Temple and the surrounding Midlothian area makes a real practical difference. They'll be familiar with the typical construction of local stone-built properties and period cottages, and they'll understand what's normal for the area's water supply and pipe infrastructure. Response times are quicker, and a local plumber is far more likely to have worked on similar properties nearby — which means fewer surprises once they're on site. If a follow-up visit is needed, you're not waiting days for someone to travel from further afield. Word-of-mouth reputation matters in a small community like Temple, which tends to keep standards high.

faqs.q: How do I know if I have a hidden leak in my Temple home?
faqs.a: Common signs include an unexplained rise in your water bill, damp or discoloured patches on walls or ceilings, the sound of running water when all taps are off, or a drop in water pressure. In older stone-built properties in Temple, visible signs can take longer to appear, so don't wait if you have a nagging suspicion something isn't right.

faqs.q: Will the plumber need to break into my walls or floors to find the leak?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. Modern leak detection equipment like acoustic sensors and thermal imaging cameras can locate many leaks without any invasive work at all. In Temple's older stone properties especially, thermal imaging is very effective. Any opening up of walls or floors would only happen once the leak is precisely located, and you'd be consulted before that work starts.

faqs.q: Can limescale from Temple's water supply cause leaks?
faqs.a: Yes, over time it can. Temple has moderately hard water, and limescale can build up inside copper pipes, creating pressure points that eventually lead to pinhole leaks — particularly on hot water pipes. It's a gradual process, but older properties with original copper pipework are more susceptible. A plumber can advise on whether your system would benefit from any protective measures.

faqs.q: How long does a leak detection and repair take in Temple?
faqs.a: For a straightforward leak in an accessible location, detection and repair can often be completed within two to three hours in a single visit. More complex situations — such as a leak buried beneath a concrete floor in a modern Temple estate home, or deep within a stone wall — may require a longer visit or a follow-up appointment once the exact location is confirmed.
